summary:
RegiÃ³n de Coquimbo stands under Chile's national framework for trans people, which is among the more developed in the region. Legal gender recognition has operated since 2019 on a self-determination basis with no medical or surgical conditions; same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022; civil unions since 2015; birth certificates have offered a third sex option since 2006; and since 2012 the criminal code has treated sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences.

The Outright International Chile country dossier, published 12 March 2026, contains no Coquimbo-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding. What can be said about this region therefore rests on Chilean law as it applies nationwide and on the regional case counts published by Movilh.

The policy direction at national level is restrictive. The Chilean congress excluded the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) from the 2026 budget bill, an action condemned by civil society groups and by the national ombuds for children.

Movilh's XXIV Annual Human Rights Report (HECHOS 2025), published March 2026, records Coquimbo at 2.62% of nationally documented abuse cases, a rise of 17.6% year-on-year in 2025.

Nationwide the same report counts a record 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression in 2025, up 27.1% and the highest total in 24 years. A mid-range regional share is not evidence of safety: documented cases rose in fourteen of the sixteen regions that year.

Trans-specific violence is documented nationally and remains a live risk for visitors. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered by an acquaintance and hidden for 24 hours; the case is treated as the country's benchmark anti-trans killing. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held for close to an hour in a transphobic attack at a hotel in Santiago, during which the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.
tangentialFactors:
Movilh reads the 2025 distribution as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate around LGBTIQ+ rights, which is the basis for treating Coquimbo's share as a mid-level signal rather than a low one. A Chilean advocacy group's annual assessment judged 2024 a year of regression for LGBTIQ+ rights, the first such reversal since the return of democracy in 1990, attributing the failure of equality and trans-rights bills to the rise of the ultra-right and to government inaction.

localsOnly:
Residents can document abuse through the channels Movilh counts: the XXIV report tabulates cases and complaints of discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and Coquimbo's 2.62% share of the 2025 national total is drawn from that regional table.

Institutional hostility is visible inside state employment. Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros in 2025 alleging that she was relegated to administrative duties, had her private life exposed without consent, and was denied support.

Gender marker changes on Chilean civil documents proceed without medical or surgical requirements, and the third sex option on birth certificates has been available since 2006.
